title: Targeted search: finding the clients that fit your service for Timber floor restoration
audience: Solo operators and team owners in any Titan Academy business who want more work from clients that suit their service, their area and their job size.
learningOutcomes: Build a prospect list that is scored against written fit criteria for service area, job size and repeat need.
Identify public signals that a client need is starting, and explain why each one is a reasonable reason to make contact.
Write a first approach that makes one specific, verifiable observation, offers one small next step and can be declined easily.

instruction.heading: Decide what work you want before you look for it
instruction.body: Write down the room sizes and floor types you restore well, the price band you can sustain, the suburbs you can reach without losing money on travel, and how often each kind of client needs you. A floor restoration is usually a one-off job per room or property, so repeat need is weaker than for a maintenance service. Say that in your criteria, and decide how you will fill the calendar between projects. These criteria are the filter for everything that follows. If you cannot state them, you cannot tell a good lead from a poor one.

instruction.heading: Build a scored prospect list
instruction.body: Keep every candidate in one list with a fit column and a status column. Score each prospect as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, using the written criteria. Ask whether it sits inside your service area, whether it has a project or repeat need, whether you can reach the person who decides, and whether the work falls within the licence and insurance you hold. The research searched for property managers, builders and trade referrals for timber floors and found no verified evidence for them, so each is a hypothesis to test. A regional business network may be a route to introductions. In Victoria, Wyndham City Council publishes a directory of local business networks, including referral groups (Wyndham City Council, undated). Record the date each entry was added and where its details came from. Use only business contact details published for business use. Do not use bought or harvested lists. ACMA's guidance says buying a list does not remove the need to show consent.

instruction.heading: Watch for signals that a need is starting
instruction.body: A signal is a public event that makes a need more likely in the near future. For timber floors, a building or planning permit can show renovation work at application or approval stage. In Victoria, some councils publish planning permit registers with suburb and status fields, such as the City of Casey register in the Victorian open data portal (DataVic, updated 5 November 2026). Check your own council's register. Victoria also publishes building permit activity by suburb or postcode, which helps you decide where to market, but it does not confirm owner or builder names (Data Vic, 28 August 2026). A permit shows that work is happening, not who will refinish the floors, so treat it as a reason to qualify, not as a prospect list. Do not turn address data into individual contact.

instruction.heading: Make a first approach that is specific and easy to decline
instruction.body: A useful first message does three things. It states how you came to know about the project. It makes one specific observation you can verify from public view or from a published notice, such as a permit for renovation works in the same street. It then offers one small next step, such as a written quote for a defined area or a fifteen-minute call. Keep the message short, do not overstate what you know, and make it simple to say no. The ACCC's 2026 review of unsolicited selling found that many approaches were pressured or misleading and that many salespeople did not identify themselves (ACCC, 28 July 2026), so a specific, honest message that names you is a practical advantage.

instruction.heading: Follow up on a fixed schedule and stop when asked
instruction.body: Decide in advance how many follow-ups you will send and how far apart. A common pattern is one reminder after a week and one final message after a further two weeks, followed by a pause. If a prospect says no, or asks you to stop, remove them from the list at once and record the request with its date. At the end of each month, review which fit tier and which signal produced replies that became paid work. Silence is not consent to keep contacting someone.

procedure: Write the room, floor type, area and repeat-need criteria for the timber work you want.
Build the prospect list and score each entry as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, with a reason.
Choose two or three public signals to watch, such as a council planning register, and note the date each one is seen.
Write one first message for each fit tier, with a stated source, one verifiable observation and one small next step.
Check each message against the electronic message rules and the licence and insurance rules for the work before sending.
Send to strong-fit prospects first, then follow up on the fixed schedule.
Remove anyone who asks you to stop, and review the results at the end of the month.

workedExamples.situation: A timber floor restorer covers three suburbs in Victoria. A planning permit for renovation works is listed on the council's register for a house in one of them. The restorer knows the owner's name from the register, and the house has no published business contact.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the restorer contact the owner now, and what should the first step be?
workedExamples.reasoning: The restorer does not contact the owner about the works just because the permit is public. The permit concerns a private house rather than a business or a public body, so it is not a basis for contacting the owner. The restorer records the permit as a reason to watch the suburb, checks whether a business or the builder has published contact details for trade work, and uses only those details. Any message that does go out names how the business learned of the works, makes one specific point and offers one small next step. The restorer does not enter the property, and does not use the owner's personal details.

equipmentAndPpe: Prospect list in a spreadsheet or notebook, with fit and status columns
Written fit criteria for service area, room type and repeat need
Message templates checked against the electronic message rules
No PPE is needed for desk work; any site visit follows the site's own safety rules

commonErrors.error: Sending the same message to everyone on a broad list at once.
commonErrors.prevention: Score the list first, write one message for each fit tier, and start with the strong-fit tier.

commonErrors.error: Using private information about an individual, such as a name from a permit, to make contact.
commonErrors.prevention: Use only contact details published for business use, or details the person has given you for this purpose.

commonErrors.error: Pitching a service that you are not licensed or insured to deliver.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the licence and insurance before outreach, and remove that service from the message.

commonErrors.error: Following up without a limit, or continuing after a request to stop. Gap: no verified property-manager or trade referral channel exists for timber floors.
commonErrors.prevention: Set a fixed number of follow-ups and a stop rule, and record every stop request.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Do not offer a licensed or authorised service in outreach unless you hold the licence that the state or territory where the work is done requires. This lesson does not grant any licence. Licence rules differ between states and territories, so check the rule for each one you work in.

Commercial electronic messages, including email and text, are regulated by the Spam Act 2003 (Cth). ACMA's Spam Act obligations page (last updated 28 March 2019) says the Act also covers business addresses, and that publishing an address does not by itself permit commercial messages. ACMA's avoid-spam guidance says marketing messages need consent, that consent should be recorded, and that unsubscribe requests must be honoured within five working days. The Act text was not read for this lesson.

Information on a public listing or a public register does not by itself permit contact about anything. If the Privacy Act applies to your business, OAIC's guidance on direct marketing (APP 7) says that public information is not exempt from the direct-marketing rules. Use only contact details published for business use, keep them secure, and stop using them when someone objects.

qualityStandard: Every prospect on the list has a fit score, a reason for that score and a recorded source for its contact details.
Every first message contains one verifiable observation and one small, easy-to-decline next step.
No contact is made using private information, and every stop request is recorded and actioned.
documentationEvidence: Prospect list with fit score, reason, status, source and date added.
Signal log with the date each public signal was seen.
Stop-request record with the date it was actioned.
summary: Define the timber work you want first, then filter prospects against that definition.
Use permit registers as reasons to qualify, and never use private information to make contact.
Gap: no verified property-manager or trade referral channel exists for timber floors. Test each prospect type before relying on it.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which prospect should you contact first?
options: A one-off job well outside your service area, because it looks large
A property manager with several properties inside your service area that you already visit
Any business that has a website, because it probably spends money on services

knowledgeChecks.question: A council register shows renovation works at a private house in your area. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Contact the homeowner using the name on the permit
Treat it as a reason to watch the area, and make contact only by a route the electronic message and do-not-call rules allow
Go onto the property to look at the floors before making contact

knowledgeChecks.question: Before you send a commercial email to a prospect, what should you do?
options: Check that the message is short enough to read on a phone and has a fun subject line
Ask the prospect to like your social media page first
Confirm the Spam Act 2003 requirements in current ACMA guidance

officialReferences.title: Avoid sending spam (ACMA)
officialReferences.covers: Says a business needs consent before sending marketing messages, and consent must be recorded; each message must identify the sender and include correct contact details; every commercial message must include an unsubscribe option that works for at least 30 days and is honoured within 5 working days. Does not name the Spam Act 2003 or cover privacy law. Publisher: ACMA.

officialReferences.title: Chapter 7: APP 7 direct marketing (OAIC)
officialReferences.pageDate: page modified 16 October 2023; version 1.1 dated 22 July 2019
officialReferences.covers: Says the direct-marketing rules apply to personal information that is publicly available, with no general exemption for public information. Applies only where the Privacy Act covers the business. Publisher: OAIC.
